name: D-Wave Revenue Reality
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Company That Actually Has Revenue
lesson.summary: D-Wave is the rare public quantum computing company with real commercial revenue, but the size and composition of that revenue tell a humbler story than the stock narrative suggests.
lesson.body:
D-Wave Quantum is unusual among public quantum computing companies: it actually has customers who pay it money. Where the broader field has been shaped by Zero Revenue Generated as the norm, D-Wave sells quantum annealer access through its Leap cloud platform, sells complete Advantage systems to a handful of buyers such as national labs, and sells professional services helping clients map problems onto annealing hardware. That is a genuine point in its favor. Having any real, paying customer base at all separates D-Wave from peers whose public materials describe only roadmaps and demonstrations.

The trouble is scale. D-Wave's annual revenue has run in the single digit millions of dollars for most of its history as a public company, occasionally reaching low double digits. Exact figures shift quarter to quarter and this text will not claim more precision than is warranted, but the order of magnitude is the point: a mid sized regional business, a car dealership group or a busy law firm, can post more annual revenue than a company marketed as building the future of computing. That gap between narrative and top line is not a rounding error, it is the entire story, and it is the same gap that will show up again once the stock's valuation is set against that revenue in the next concept.

Composition matters as much as size. A meaningful share of that revenue has historically come from professional services and government contracts rather than repeatable product sales. Services revenue means billed hours: a consulting engagement, a national lab contract to explore one specific use case. That kind of revenue does not scale the way a software subscription does, doubling it generally means doubling headcount and cost, not just running the same code for twice as many customers. When judging any technology company's top line, always ask whether the dollars are one time and labor intensive or recurring and scalable, and whether the customer base is growing or simply cycling through a small pool of research minded early adopters. D-Wave's revenue leans toward the former on both counts.

This is where D-Wave Exaggerated Claims meets commercial reality. Announcements describing quantum supremacy demonstrations and large speedups on narrow optimization benchmarks sit alongside a company with real but tiny, services heavy revenue. A skeptic should credit revenue existing at all, then immediately ask three follow up questions: how large is the number in absolute terms, how fast is it growing year over year, and how much is recurring versus one off. D-Wave clears the first bar and struggles on the other two, which sets up the next problem entirely.

This modest, services heavy figure becomes the denominator in every valuation multiple that follows. A small, low quality denominator is exactly what turns a valuation multiple into triple or quadruple digits, which is the subject taken up next under Market Valuation vs Revenue.
